purpose: This medicine is used to treat Pompe disease, a rare inherited condition where a specific enzyme is missing or not working properly. Without this enzyme, a sugar called glycogen builds up and damages muscles, including the heart and breathing muscles. This medication helps replace the missing enzyme so your body can break down that sugar buildup.
how_it_works: Your body normally makes an enzyme called acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) that breaks down glycogen stored in your cells. In Pompe disease, this enzyme is missing or does not work well, causing glycogen to pile up and damage muscle cells. This medication is a lab-made version of that enzyme, given through an IV infusion, so it can do the job your body cannot do on its own.
common_side_effects: Infusion reactions such as flushing, hives, rash, nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness, fever, chills, fatigue, or feeling cold during or after the infusion. Some patients may also notice muscle or joint pain.
warnings: Serious allergic reactions, including life-threatening anaphylaxis, can happen during infusions — medical staff will monitor you closely each time. Infusion reactions are common, and your doctor may give you pre-medications such as antihistamines or steroids to reduce this risk. Tell your doctor right away if you have trouble breathing, chest tightness, swelling, or feel very unwell during your infusion.
typical_dosing: This medication is given as an IV (intravenous) infusion in a clinic or infusion center, typically once every two weeks. The dose is based on your body weight. Each infusion takes several hours, and the rate may be slowly increased over time as your body tolerates it. Your healthcare team will determine the right dose and schedule for you.
